title: Connectedness detected by representations with zero differential
statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field], and let $H$ be an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. For a finite-dimensional rational representation $r:H\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ [def-wf-algebraic-representations], its differential $dr:\operatorname{Lie}(H)\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)$ is induced on the kernels of reduction of dual-number points; $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ is the tangent Lie algebra at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space, def-sc-dual-numbers, def-wf-lie-algebra, def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation]. Then $H$ is geometrically connected if and only if every such representation with $dr=0$ is trivial. Geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure, with connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Trivial means $r_A(h)=1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and every $h\in H(A)$. The zero vector space is allowed.

source.place: Note 9.50, printed pp.184--185 (finite quotients detect components in characteristic zero), and Proposition 10.31 with Cartier 3.23 and Proposition 10.15, printed pp.196,71,190--191. This precise zero-differential formulation is an agent-stated consequence of those general criteria.

proof.text: Assume $H$ geometrically connected. By [lem-weil-geometrically-connected-algebraic-closure] it is connected (take the extension $k/k$), and by [lem-sfb-cartier-characteristic-zero-smooth] it is smooth. Let $r$ have $dr=0$. If $V=0$, its automorphism group on every algebra is the singleton, so the conclusion holds. Otherwise choose a basis of $V$ of size $n\geq1$. In the coordinate presentation of [def-sc-general-linear-group], the identity subgroup $E=\operatorname{Spec}k\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ is cut out by $x_{ij}-\delta_{ij}$; its coordinate map onto $k$ is surjective, so [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion] makes it a closed subgroup. Its tangent space is zero: its only dual-number point over its identity is its identity. Thus $dr(\operatorname{Lie}(H))=0\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(E)$. Apply [lem-sfb-charzero-lie-detects-factorization] to factor $r$ through $E$. This gives $r_A(h)=I_n$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Cartier 3.23, p.71; 10.14 and Proposition 10.15, pp.190--191, applied to the identity subgroup; coordinate description 2.8, p.41. Stacks Tag 047N supplies the cited Cartier theorem.

proof.text: For the converse put $P=\Pi_k(H)$ and $q=q_H$ from [lem-sfb-algebraic-scheme-etale-components]. Its separatedness hypothesis holds by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-source-morphism-separated], since $H$ is affine. The product comparisons and functoriality in the component-scheme statement give a group law $m_P=\Pi_k(m_H)$, inverse $\Pi_k(i_H)$, and identity $\Pi_k(e_H)$ after identifying $\Pi_k(H\times H)=P\times P$ and $\Pi_k(\operatorname{Spec}k)=\operatorname{Spec}k$. Applying this functor to the associativity, unit and inverse diagrams of $H$ gives the corresponding diagrams for $P$; naturality says $q$ commutes with these operations. Consequently $P$ is a finite etale $k$-group scheme and $q$ a group homomorphism. The nonempty-fibre clause makes $q$ surjective on underlying spaces. The definition [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] makes $P$ affine with finite-dimensional coordinate algebra $B$; it is of finite type because a finite vector-space spanning set of $B$ also generates $B$ as a $k$-algebra.

source.place: Propositions 1.30--1.31 and Remark 1.33, pp.15--16; construction of the group structure before Proposition 2.37 and its proof, pp.51--52.

proof.text: Since $P$ is etale, [def-weil-etale-morphism] makes it unramified. Apply the forward implication of [lem-sfb-group-scheme-identity-dual-unramified] to $P$: every dual-number point reducing to the identity is the identity. Hence $\operatorname{Lie}(P)=0$. By [lem-sfb-finite-group-faithful-regular-matrices], the right regular action on the finite-dimensional vector space $B=k[P]$ is a representation $\rho:P\to\operatorname{GL}(B)$ and its coordinate homomorphism is surjective. The space $B$ is nonzero, since the identity of $P$ gives a unital map $B\to k$. Form the rational representation $r=\rho\circ q$ of $H$ on $B$. The differential composition formula in [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] gives $dr=d\rho\circ dq=0$, because $dq$ takes values in $\operatorname{Lie}(P)=0$.

source.place: Note 9.50 and preceding 9.49, pp.184--185, using the regular representation of 4.9, p.87, and functoriality of Lie in 10.5--10.6. Etale dual-number uniqueness: Stacks Tags 047I and 02G5 as in the cited group-scheme criterion.

proof.text: Assume now that every zero-differential representation of $H$ is trivial. Apply this assumption to the $r$ of step 3. For every $k$-algebra $A$ and $h\in H(A)$, we obtain $\rho_A(q_A(h))=I=\rho_A(e_P)$. The surjectivity of the coordinate map supplied by [lem-sfb-finite-group-faithful-regular-matrices] implies that $\rho_A$ is injective: two algebra maps $B\to A$ agreeing after precomposition with a surjection into $B$ agree on every element of $B$. Thus $q_A(h)=e_P$ for all $A,h$. In particular take $A=k[H]$ and the universal point given by its identity algebra map. This shows that the coordinate map of $q$ equals that of $e_P\circ(H\to\operatorname{Spec}k)$, so $q$ is the constant identity morphism of schemes, rather than just constant on $k$-points.

source.place: Note 9.50, pp.184--185, with the faithful regular representation of 4.9, p.87; explicit all-algebras faithfulness and universal-point argument.

proof.text: The surjectivity of $q$ in step 2 and its constancy in step 4 imply that $|P|$ consists only of its identity point. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product] to its affine coordinate algebra: $B\cong\prod_{j=1}^s L_j$ with $L_j/k$ finite separable fields. The spectrum of this product has one point for each factor (a prime contains exactly all but one of the orthogonal coordinate idempotents), so $s=1$; $s=0$ is excluded by the identity point. The identity section gives a $k$-algebra map $L_1\to k$. This map is injective because its domain is a field, and its image contains $k$, so $L_1=k$. Hence $P\cong\operatorname{Spec}k$. The nonempty geometrically connected fibre assertion of [lem-sfb-algebraic-scheme-etale-components] now applies to its sole fibre, which is all of $H$. It proves that $H$ is geometrically connected, completing the converse over the original field $k$.

source.place: Proposition 1.31(b) and Corollary 1.32, p.16; Proposition 2.37(d) and Remark 2.39(a), pp.51--52; Note 9.50, pp.184--185. Etale algebras over a field: Stacks Tag 00U3.

Step 1 meets every hypothesis of the factorization lemma: H is smooth (Cartier) and connected (the algebraic-closure test with k'=k); E=Spec k is a closed subgroup of GL_n by the affine closed-immersion criterion; Lie E=0; dr equals df_e. Step 3: étale gives unramified, the forward direction of the dual-number criterion gives Lie P=0, the regular representation exists for finite P, and the composition clause gives d(ρq)=0. Step 4: the surjective coordinate map plus the U-specialization clause make ρ_A injective, and the universal point gives q constant as a morphism. Step 5: an étale algebra with one point and a k-point is k, and the single fibre (all of H) is geometrically connected. Small cases checked: H=1, V=0, G_a and G_m, constant Z/2 (sign character), μ_3/Q, and the char-p Frobenius counterexample showing char 0 is needed.
